mcqs.question: Three components sit in sequence on a request's critical path, with availabilities 99.9%, 99.5%, and 99%. How do you compute the chain's overall availability?
options: Add the three percentages and divide by 3
Take the minimum of the three values
Take the maximum of the three values
mcqs.explanation: A serial dependency is only as available as the product of its links, since every request must pass through all of them successfully. Averaging, or taking the min/max, doesn't reflect that all three must independently succeed for the request to succeed.

mcqs.question: A database node is 90% available on its own. Adding one identical redundant replica in parallel brings the pair's availability to approximately what?
options: 90% — redundancy doesn't change a single node's own reliability
99% — the pair only fails if both nodes fail at the same time
81% — multiply the two nodes' availabilities together like a serial chain
mcqs.explanation: Redundancy math (1-(1-p)^n) applies because the parallel pair only fails when every copy fails simultaneously: 1-(1-0.1)^2 = 0.99. Multiplying like a serial chain (81%) would be wrong here — that formula is for components a request must pass through in sequence, not redundant copies of the same thing.

mcqs.question: In a chain of load balancer (99.99%), app server (99.95%), and database (99.9%), which component should you invest in improving first to raise end-to-end availability the most?
options: The load balancer, since it's first in the request path
The database, since it's the lowest-availability link on the critical path
All three equally, since they contribute equally to the product
The app server, since it sits in the middle of the chain
mcqs.explanation: The chain's total availability is bounded by its weakest serial link, so improving the database — already the lowest number — has the most leverage. Position in the chain (first, middle) doesn't matter to the math; only each component's own availability does.

mcqs.question: A candidate says "we'll target 99.99% availability" with no component numbers, while a third-party payments API on the critical path is contractually capped at 99.9%. What's wrong with the claim?
options: Nothing — 99.99% is always achievable with enough engineering effort
The claim is fine, since third-party dependencies don't count toward availability math
The claim would only be wrong if the payments API were on a parallel, not serial, path
The claim ignores that a serial dependency capped at 99.9% makes 99.99% end-to-end mathematically impossible
mcqs.explanation: A serial chain's ceiling is set by its worst link — if a required dependency tops out at 99.9%, no amount of effort elsewhere lets the end-to-end number exceed that. Third-party dependencies on the critical path absolutely count, and this is exactly the serial (not parallel) case where the cap applies.
